planting.note: Plant container shrubs in early spring in moist, very well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; this compact botanical variety fits nicely at the front of a woodland or ericaceous border where its darker flowers can be viewed up close.

directions: This naturally dwarf botanical variety of redvein enkianthus stays notably more compact and dense than the species, making it a fit for smaller gardens or the front of an ericaceous border. In late spring it bears clusters of small, urn-shaped flowers in a deeper reddish-purple than typical campanulatus forms, followed by dependable orange-to-scarlet fall color on fine-textured foliage. Grow in consistently moist, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade alongside rhododendrons and azaleas, and avoid letting the shallow, fibrous roots dry out during summer. Its slow growth means little pruning is needed beyond removing dead wood.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade or a sheltered woodland opening; this Himalayan species is more vigorous and less reliably cold-hardy than redvein enkianthus, so site it out of harsh winter wind.

directions: Native to the Himalaya and into western China, this vigorous, upright species is the largest-growing member of the genus in cultivation, eventually forming a large shrub or small tree with glossy foliage that colors red and orange in autumn. In late spring and early summer it produces hanging clusters of cream, pink-veined, urn-shaped flowers that are comparatively the largest of any enkianthus. Grow in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil in partial shade or a lightly open woodland site, and give it room to develop its eventual small-tree stature. It is less cold-hardy than Enkianthus campanulatus and benefits from a sheltered position in the colder end of its range.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; this southern-China-to-Myanmar species needs a milder climate than redvein enkianthus and appreciates protection from hard freezes.

directions: Native from southern China to Myanmar, Chinese enkianthus is a deciduous shrub or small tree with foliage clustered at the branch tips in the manner typical of the genus. Terminal umbels of larger, more vividly orange-red bell flowers appear in late spring, showier than the paler blooms of redvein enkianthus, followed by good autumn foliage color. It requires the same moist, acidic, humus-rich soil and partial shade as its relatives but is markedly less cold-hardy, so reserve it for milder gardens or a warm, sheltered microclimate. Established plants need little care beyond mulching to conserve soil moisture and buffer root-zone temperatures.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; this compact, slow-growing Weston Nursery selection suits a foundation planting or the middle layer of an ericaceous border where its heavier flower display can be appreciated up close.

directions: Selected by Ed Mezitt of Weston Nursery, 'Showy Lantern' is a compact, densely branched redvein enkianthus cultivar prized for producing an unusually heavy display of pendulous, bell-shaped flowers in creamy pink streaked with deep red, opening in mid-to-late spring and attracting bees. Its narrow, upright habit and slower growth keep it smaller than the species, and its neat foliage turns scarlet in autumn for a strong second season of interest. Grow in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to light sun alongside azaleas and rhododendrons, and avoid soils that dry out or turn alkaline. Little pruning is required beyond removing dead or crossing wood after flowering.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; give this slower-growing, large-flowered selection an open woodland-garden site where its outsized blooms can hang free of surrounding foliage.

directions: 'Venus' is a slower-growing redvein enkianthus selection distinguished by unusually large, pendent clusters of five to fifteen bell-shaped cream flowers flushed and veined in red, opening in late spring and early summer well above the emerging foliage. Its eventual spreading, small-tree habit and fiery orange-and-red autumn color make it a striking specimen in an open woodland garden. Grow in humus-rich, moist but well-drained, acidic to neutral soil in full sun or partial shade, siting it where the oversized flower clusters are visible from below. Because it grows more slowly than the species, it is a good choice where a long-term, well-behaved specimen shrub is wanted rather than a fast screen.
